transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-03
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes (scheduled)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Arjun Rao (Redwood SE), Nina Alvarez (Harbor Grove CTO), Marcus Reed (Lead ML Eng), Sophie Lang (Infra), Omar Diaz (Product)

Summary (auto): quick discovery to understand Harbor Grove's p95 latency and throughput targets, explore Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for streaming use cases, plan a pilot and benchmark run.

Topics: p95 targets, streaming-first token/sec benchmarks, concurrency profile, batching/caching trade-offs, security/compliance (SOC2, KMS, VPC), next steps for pilot.

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh can we do quick intros? im Maya, AE at Redwood.
[00:12] Nina: nina here, CTO at Harbor Grove, thanks for setting this up.
[00:16] Marcus: Marcus, lead ML eng, i own model infra and perf.
[00:19] Sophie: Sophie, infra, net and security.
[00:21] Omar: Omar, product.
[00:25] Liam: Liam Patel, Redwood SE - ill cover benchmarks and test harness.
[00:30] Maya: awesome, high level we heard youre building a streaming assistant for maritime ops, need low p95 on first token and sustained throughput for bursts. want to confirm the numbers, Nina?
[00:41] Nina: yeah that's right. we have two main flows: quick assist (short prompts, 50-150 tokens) and deep debrief (long, 1k-3k tokens). target for quick assist is p95 first token under 250ms, ideally under 200ms for hosted, but were open on dedicated if cost gets out of hand.
[01:03] Marcus: for deep debriefs we care more about steady tokens/sec and end-to-end tail for full response - p95 end-to-end under 3s for 2k token responses would be nice but it's flexible. concurrency - typical active users 150-200 concurrent streams at peak, with burst windows up to 600 concurrent for 30-90s during system-wide alerts.
[01:28] Liam: ok that's helpful. are those 150-200 long-lived streaming connections or short calls? streaming concurrency has different implications for token generation vs batch throughput.
[01:38] Marcus: streaming - yes long-lived, each user sees tokens in real time, so we need low first byte and stable per-token latency. token rate per stream roughly 10-15 tokens/sec during streaming for the longer responses.
[01:50] Arjun: if i may, the two big levers are model selection & quantization, and serving topology — continuous batching helps throughput but can add latency if batch windows are too large. prefix/KV cache and warm-hot pools can reduce the first-token cost.
[02:06] Sophie: security notes - were regulated, need SOC2 Type II, SAML SSO, audit logs, and the option to keep logs in our VPC. private deployment would be preferred if Redwood can support HSM or KMS integration for keys.
[02:21] Maya: we do have SOC2, SSO integrations, and KMS support - for Private we support customer KMS in the private plane. small note - sometimes our docs say customer-managed KMS with HSM gateways depending on on-prem setup, but we can share certs.
[02:35] Nina: okay good. cost wise, can you give a rough comparison Dedicated vs Hosted for this profile?
[02:41] Maya: top-level: Hosted is simplest and lower short-term friction, Dedicated gives predictable throughput and capacity isolation - its cheaper per token at scale if you commit, and Private is for regulatory/networking needs. for bursts you can combine Dedicated with burst pools in Hosted for overflow. we can send a side-by-side later.
[02:59] Liam: for numbers, rough back-of-envelope: with a 40 token/second GPU effective throughput for a 13B quantized model you might support X concurrent streams at Y p95 — but ill run exact sims with your prompt set. we typically advise running a 2-phase benchmark: single-stream/first-token profiling and then scaled concurrency with realistic inter-arrival times.
[03:19] Marcus: well send sample prompts. question: were leaning towards Llama-derivative 34B quantized or 13B for price, any guidance about streaming vs batching?
[03:29] Arjun: larger models increase per-token compute and thus reduce tokens/sec but may improve output quality. for real-time streaming, 13B quantized to int8 or int4 often hits better latency targets with good quality. 34B is possible but youd likely need more GPUs and dedicated capacity for our p95 goals.
[03:44] Nina: what about quantization risks - hallucinations or quality drops?
[03:48] Arjun: there's trade-offs; we recommend Redwood Optimize runs: model-aware quant profiles and a small eval set to monitor quality regressions tied to your prompt sets. can flag if int4 causes issues.
[03:57] [04:00] Omar: for the burst scenario - 600 concurrent for 30-90s - is that something Redwoods autoscaling can absorb or do we need reserved capacity?
[04:08] Liam: autoscaling can manage some of that but cold-starts for new capacity impact p95. solution: reserved Dedicated capacity sized for your steady-state (150-200) with a burst policy to use hosted pools for overflow. that keeps steady p95 low and handles short spikes. you can also pre-warm a buffer pool if you expect predictable windows.
[04:25] Sophie: networking detail: we need low egress latency inside our AWS region; can Redwood deploy Dedicated in our VPC or do we have to reverse-proxy through your endpoints?
[04:34] Maya: Dedicated can be colocated in customer VPC or run in our dedicated tenancy depending on contract. for Private on-prem, we ship the private plane. well include topology diagrams in the follow-up.
[04:44] Marcus: measurement methods - what metrics should we capture during the pilot to decide fit?
[04:49] Liam: main metrics: first-byte latency (first token), per-token latency distribution, p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec per GPU, queue times, batch sizes, KV cache hit rates, and cost per 1k tokens. instrument both client-side (end-to-end) and server-side (model exec).
[05:03] Nina: do you have an example perf harness we can reuse?
[05:06] Liam: yes, ill share our benchmark harness (github link) — it supports open loop and closed loop tests, synthetic token rates, and replay of real traces. we can adapt it to your prompt set.
[05:14] Marcus: sample prompt set well provide includes typical 80-150 token quick assists, and two deep flows of about 1.5k and 2.8k tokens.
[05:23] Arjun: perfect - for the deep flows well test streaming chunk sizes and server-side chunking strategy to keep p95 acceptable while avoiding huge memory/KV cache spikes.
[05:33] Nina: SLA expectations - we need guidance on achievable SLOs per deployment type.
[05:37] Maya: for Hosted we typically quote p95 first-byte in 200-400ms range depending on model/ctx; Dedicated can be tuned for lower p95 with reserved slots. Private on-prem can hit the lowest network latency but depends on your infra. SLA for Dedicated includes a throughput target if you reserve capacity.
[05:55] Sophie: curious about prefix or KV cache - can Redwood cache user prefixes to reduce compute for repeated queries?
[06:02] Liam: yes, prefix/KV caching is supported - it caches transformer key-value states for repeated context so repeated prompts with similar prefixes can be served faster. that helps heavily for short prompts that share history. cache hit rates will be a key metric in the pilot.
[06:14] Marcus: any notes on batching window and continuous batching - were worried about batching adding 50-100ms of extra tail latency sometimes.
[06:22] Arjun: batching is workload sensitive. continuous batching with micro-batches can keep latency low while boosting throughput; you can configure max batch wait and max batch size per route. Redwood's runtime also does kernel selection to reduce time for streaming-friendly models.
[06:35] Nina: do you support sending function calls in streaming and still maintain low p95?
[06:40] Liam: yes but function/tool calling sometimes increases per-token compute (extra parsing/structure). well test that specifically. real-world function-call payloads can increase latency a bit but not dramatically for most flows.
[06:51] Omar: about observability—can we get token-level tracing and per-request cost breakdowns?
[06:57] Maya: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost, per-route latency breakdown, and traces; you can also integrate with Datadog or internal tracing. for pilot we'll open access to a dashboard.
[07:07] Marcus: great. for the benchmark we want the SEs to run a scenario: 200 steady streams with bursts to 600, two model variants (13B int8 and 34B int8), and streaming enabled with 10 tokens/sec per stream. can Redwood simulate that?
[07:19] Liam: yes - well run both steady and spike scenarios, measure first-token p95, sustained per-token latency, GPU utilization, and tokens/sec. well also test Dedicated baseline + hosted overflow.
[07:30] Nina: question re: throttling and fair-share. during spikes, we cant drop critical command flows. how does Redwood do prioritization?
[07:37] Arjun: routing policies can prioritize by route or API key; you can have priority lanes for critical flows, automatic fallback to smaller model variants, and canary rollouts. fallback to a cheaper/shorter model variant is common to preserve availability.
[07:50] Sophie: encryption at rest and in transit? KMS options?
[07:54] Maya: TLS for in-transit; at-rest encryption with customer KMS for Dedicated/Private. we support customer-managed keys and HSMs in private deployments. audit logs go to the console and optional log export to your SIEM.
[08:06] Marcus: do you have examples of token/sec per GPU for popular open models?
[08:11] Liam: ballpark - for a modern 8-bit quantized 13B you might see 20-50 tokens/sec per GPU depending on sequence length and kernel. 34B is closer to 5-15 tokens/sec per GPU. again, depends on sequence length and attention patterns.
[08:27] Nina: ok that helps. question on metrics collection: will you provide server metrics or do we instrument?
[08:32] Liam: both. well provide server-side telemetry and opaque metrics, but recommend instrumenting client side for end-to-end SLOs. well share dashboard templates.
[08:44] [09:00] (brief cross-talk about calendar invites and logistics)
[09:15] Omar: slightly concerned about cost for 34B - do you have per-token estimates?
[09:20] Maya: we'll send a detailed pricing sheet but high-level 34B can be 2-4x more expensive than 13B per token; Dedicated reduces unit cost if you reserve GPUs. we'll include model/quant-targeted pricing scenarios.
[09:33] Marcus: let's talk fallback behavior - we want guaranteed availability of critical flows even if some capacity is saturated. is there a built-in circuit breaker?
[09:40] Arjun: yes - you can define fallbacks per route: reject, queue, or downgrade to a lower-cost model. Redwood also offers request-level timeouts and can automatically reroute to another region or model family.
[09:53] Nina: what's typical p95 improvement if we go Dedicated and pre-warm cache vs Hosted?
[09:59] Liam: depends, but pre-warmed Dedicated with prefix cache can cut first-token p95 by 30-60% compared to a cold-hosted path in some cases. again, will quantify in the pilot.
[10:12] Sophie: on the private deployment path - are there clients who run the private plane inside their AWS accounts?
[10:18] Maya: yes - a few enterprise customers run the control plane in their environment with us managing software; others have fully on-prem installs. we can discuss the architecture patterns.
[10:29] Marcus: ok lets nail down the pilot steps.
[10:33] Maya: proposed pilot: 2-week bench harness run - week 1: single-stream and first-token profiling; week 2: scaled concurrency + burst scenarios. Redwood provides SE time to run tests and analyze results. deliverable: perf report with p50/p95/p99, GPU tokens/sec, cost model, and suggested Dedicated sizing.
[10:51] Nina: that's acceptable. how long to set up the Dedicated reserved pool?
[10:55] Maya: provisioning Dedicated typically takes 2-4 weeks depending on contract and region; pilot can be done on Hosted with a reserved test pool to mimic Dedicated while procurement completes.
[11:06] Omar: procurement/contracting - we need standard security addenda and a BAA possibility.
[11:11] Maya: weve got templates for security addenda, SOC2 reports, and BAA - ill share them in the follow-up.
[11:18] Sophie: are there network egress considerations during benchmarks?
[11:22] Liam: yes - well co-ordinate region placement and can enable private peering for low-latency tests. well include network latency baselines in the report.
[11:33] Marcus: for the scaled test, what metrics do you need from us?
[11:37] Liam: your prompt set, expected concurrency timeline (traffic pattern), and any special features like function calling or tool usage. also whether you need EU-only residency.
[11:47] Nina: we need EU residency for data in production, but pilot can be run in us-east.
[11:52] Maya: fine. well note that.
[11:55] [12:30] (discussion about sample schedule and when the SEs can run)
[13:00] Marcus: would you recommend trying int4 quant for 13B to squeeze more tokens/sec?
[13:06] Arjun: int4 can boost throughput but test for quality regressions; well run an eval set. often int8 is a safer first pass.
[13:15] Nina: anything else you need from our side to scope the Dedicated sizing?
[13:18] Liam: your steady-state concurrency (150-200), average token rates, and percent of streaming vs single-turn. also target p95 numbers youd accept per route.
[13:29] Marcus: were comfortable with: quick assist p95 first-token <= 250ms, deep debrief end-to-end p95 <= 3s, steady 150-200 concurrent streams, bursts to 600.
[13:40] Maya: perfect. well model cost and capacity for those numbers.
[13:44] Omar: curious, what's Redwood's approach to runtime kernel selection you mentioned earlier?
[13:48] Liam: the runtime inspects model architecture and sequence length and picks optimized kernels and attention implementations; that helps smooth out tail latencies for certain length distributions.
[13:57] Sophie: are there any limits on streaming chunk size?
[14:00] Arjun: not strict limits but we recommend 16-64 token chunks for most clients; smaller chunks increase request overhead, bigger chunks increase jitter/latency per token.
[14:10] Nina: ok timeline - we want benchmarks + decision in ~3 weeks. is that realistic?
[14:15] Maya: yes, pilot run + report in 2-3 weeks if you can deliver the prompt set and confirm contact points.
[14:21] [14:40] (brief mute while documents are shared)
[15:00] Marcus: one more question - what about multi-region failover for availability?
[15:05] Liam: Redwood supports multi-region routing and active-passive failover; for low-latency needs we recommend colocating Dedicated in primary region and setting regional failover policies.
[15:17] Nina: good.
[15:20] Omar: do you have customers who do hybrid Dedicated+Private for compliance?
[15:25] Maya: yes some enterprises use Private for PII-sensitive flows and Dedicated for general-purpose low-latency inference. we can share references under NDA.
[15:34] Marcus: regarding cost modeling, will Redwood include estimated GPU counts and commit levels?
[15:38] Maya: yes - the sizing report will have recommended GPU pool size, estimated LCU or commit, and projected unit economics at expected throughput.
[15:47] [16:00] (wrap up)
[16:05] Maya: ok to recap: action items - harbor grove to send prompts and traffic pattern by 2027-08-05; Redwood to send pilot pricing, security docs, and benchmark harness by 2027-08-06; schedule the benchmark week of 2027-08-09.
[16:20] Nina: sounds good. thanks all.
[16:23] Maya: thanks everyone, talk soon.
[16:28] (call ends)
